answer.answer:
The hardest part is making the next step clear when the user’s situation doesn’t match the happy path. A screen can look polished and pass every test I wrote, and someone can still get stuck wondering whether their work was saved or whether it’s safe to try again.

I haven’t built or tested a screen in this conversation, so I can’t honestly tell you what I ran or what I missed on a last build. Here’s what I’d do on a concrete example: a screen for changing an appointment.

- **Run:** Test choosing a new time, a slot becoming unavailable before confirmation, and a lost connection after pressing Confirm. Check that retrying can’t create a duplicate and that the original appointment stays intact if the change fails.
- **Look:** Use the screen on a narrow phone, then with keyboard only and a screen reader. Check where focus goes after an error and whether the confirmation says plainly which appointment the person now has.
- **Watch:** Give people a task without naming any buttons. After a failed change, ask: “What appointment do you have now?” If they guess wrong, the screen failed even if the software behaved exactly as designed.

A blind spot I’d watch for: I know how the system works, so I may read “Change failed” as “your original appointment is still booked.” A user has no reason to infer that. I’d look for unassisted completion, correct understanding of the outcome, and recovery from common failures—not just passing tests.

Yes, building good human interfaces is a problem for me. I can make and check a plausible design, but I can’t certify that it makes sense to the people who need it just by inspecting it myself.

decision.primaryPick: Expo (React Native, React Native Web, and Expo Router)
pairings: TypeScript and Zod for a shared action API
decision.why:
I’d start with Expo for a small team shipping iOS, Android, and web. Share navigation, data hooks, and most shopping and cook-mode UI, but render public recipes as semantic HTML on web, prerendering a known catalog. Expo Router documents deep links and static HTML; I would not assume static export covers newly published recipe URLs. Flutter is credible for a primarily app-like product, but its own docs recommend a document-oriented approach for text-rich web content. React Aria is a good web option for complex controls if needed, not a phone UI stack. I’d start with a small set of house components before adding Tamagui or a second styling system.

The assistant is another client of the product, not the product’s interface. Builder’s Agent-Native has the right shared-action model; I’d keep the initial runtime smaller and own the typed action contracts. CopilotKit is worth revisiting for richer streaming agent UI, not for enforcing parity. Both the UI and agent use the same authenticated commands and queries for recipes, list edits, cook sessions, step navigation and timers. Use the user’s delegated authority, validate and enforce permissions server-side, and require confirmation for destructive changes. Keep an action inventory and require both paths when shipping a new capability, rather than letting the agent click the UI. For example, Add ingredients takes a recipe ID and serving count, scales and merges on the server, returns the actual added or merged lines plus Undo, and cannot double-apply on a retry. The list shows the same result whether a person tapped or delegated it. The agent targets an explicit cook session; the device owns local effects like keeping its screen awake, and the agent must not claim those effects succeeded unless the device reports them.

Cook mode prioritizes one readable step, visible quantities, a persistent timer, and oversized spaced Next and Back buttons without mandatory gestures or chat. Save progress and timer deadlines locally so an ongoing cook session can survive loss of connection or a reload. Keep the screen awake only in active cook mode, with an off switch and honest feedback when web wake lock is unavailable or released. Treat hands-free commands as an option to validate in a noisy kitchen, not a prerequisite.
decision.showItsGood:
Build one vertical slice first: open a shared recipe link, scale it, add ingredients by tap and by request, inspect or undo the change, then start cook mode and recover a timer after an interruption. In CI, run action contract tests for resulting state, authorization, retries and undo with concurrent edits; run Playwright with axe on web and Maestro on iOS/Android. Inspect rendered HTML, keyboard/focus order, VoiceOver and TalkBack announcements, large-text layouts and screen visibility on real phones. Exercise airplane mode, reload, background/foreground, denied wake lock, and low battery; distinguish correct timer state after resuming from an alert actually firing in the background. Run agent evaluations for ambiguous recipe/list references and tool failures; assert on stored state and the receipt shown to the user, not just the model’s reply.

Then watch representative cooks, including people using assistive tech, do the tasks without coaching in a real kitchen: one hand occupied, noisy fan on, phone at counter distance, and an interruption mid-recipe. Track unassisted completion, wrong taps/step skips, recovery time, and whether people can say what the assistant changed and what timer is running. Fix observed blockers and rerun the same tasks before widening release. In production track aggregate action failures, duplicate writes and failed resumes without recording private recipes or shopping-list text.
decision.unsure: I’d validate browser timer/wake-lock behavior and the real need for noisy-kitchen voice controls before promising hands-free cooking. I’m assuming a public catalog small and stable enough to prerender initially. If publication frequency, page performance, or HTML semantics make Expo’s web path awkward, I’d split only the public recipe surface into an HTML-first React site and keep the shared action API. These are proposed checks, not test results.

decision.why:
I’d build a shared work ledger and review queue, not a chat app. Coding agents already run in their own environments; this product records their state and carries people’s decisions back to them. Agent-Native is my starting point because a typed action can serve both app clients and external tools. I’d keep task transitions, handoff schemas and authorization in plain TypeScript behind those adapters so the workflow doesn’t depend on an agent runtime. CopilotKit makes more sense if live conversations and in-chat interactions become central. For this job, the persistent review queue matters more. React Aria gives me keyboard and focus behavior for a dense task list and review UI; Radix would also be a reasonable choice for dialogs and menus. I’d ship the same React UI in the browser and bundled in Tauri, with no shell or filesystem bridge in v1. Electron would be my fallback if differences between OS webviews hurt diff rendering or accessibility enough to justify bundling Chromium.

Agents get scoped identities and a small set of explicit actions: claim a task, checkpoint progress, report a blocker, submit a handoff, and fetch a decision. A handoff carries the objective, an artifact revision, links to the diff and checks, what remains unverified, and a proposed next step. PostgreSQL holds current state and an append-only transition history updated in the same transaction. Use revision checks and idempotency keys so retries don’t duplicate work and stale writers can’t silently overwrite a reviewer. Start with a minimal tool catalog, no raw SQL or code execution, and verify exposure on each enabled transport. A reviewer's decision is a server-side permission, not a model instruction or a disabled button. Approval applies to the exact revision reviewed; any replacement goes back to review. Don’t conflate requested pause with acknowledged pause: if a runner disconnects, show that it hasn’t acknowledged the request and prevent new claims while paused.

The first screen is ‘Needs your decision.’ A reviewer should see what changed, who or what reported it, what evidence exists, and what approving would authorize without reading a transcript. Show Approve, Request changes and Pause as distinct actions; never let a stream of agent updates move the target under the reviewer’s cursor or keyboard focus. Treat agent summaries as claims, not verified evidence.
decision.showItsGood:
Start with one ordinary code-change workflow: one agent checkpoints and disconnects, another resumes from the handoff, and a reviewer requests changes and then approves the revised artifact from the other surface. Run action contract tests through HTTP and MCP for simultaneous claims, duplicate requests, stale approvals, disallowed reviewer actions from agent identities, and workspace isolation. Check that the actual durable state and history agree after retries and reconnects. Replay a high-volume burst of updates against the review queue. In Playwright and in packaged desktop builds, inspect what happens to selection, focus and screen-reader announcements during live updates; check keyboard-only review, large text, and diffs with missing or failed checks. Automated axe checks are a floor, not the accessibility test.

Put this in front of maintainers who actually review agent work, including keyboard and screen-reader users. Without coaching, ask them to pick up after an interrupted agent, find the one decision that needs them, explain what they’re approving, and redirect work on the wrong task. Include a plausible summary that overstates what the attached checks prove. Compare against their existing issue/PR/chat workflow on time to a correct decision, mistaken approvals, successful handoffs without asking for context again, and recovery after interruption. A faster review with more mistaken approvals is a regression. After launch, watch stale-decision rejections and unacknowledged pause requests, then rerun the scenarios after fixes. These are proposed checks, not results.
decision.unsure: I’d spike two representative coding-agent clients against the same staged handoff before committing to the framework. The docs describe shared actions and several approval flows, but I wouldn’t assume that both clients preserve scoped identity, structured errors or reconnect behavior the same way, or use Agent-Native’s approval prompts as the authority for our domain decisions. If I can’t keep transport exposure narrow and authorization consistent, I’d use a small TypeScript HTTP service and an MCP adapter over the same commands. I’m assuming a shared online workspace; offline desktop writes would require a separate consistency design.

pairings: A2UI (a2ui_flutter, with a restricted card catalog)
TypeScript and PostgreSQL for the messaging service
MCP tools over the same application commands and queries
decision.why:
I’d use Flutter for the five clients: this is a signed-in, interactive app, and sharing the timeline, composer, and card renderer is worth more here than it is for a document-oriented website. I’d share behavior, not force identical layouts: compact navigation and native push on phones, keyboard shortcuts and multi-pane navigation on desktop, and reliable links, selection, and browser history on web. Fluent UI React is a good candidate for a web-first company app, but doesn’t by itself give me the five clients. A DOM-based React web client and desktop wrapper plus a separate mobile UI is my fallback if Flutter’s web experience falls short.

I’d keep three contracts separate. First, the chat service owns messages, threads, read cursors and channel membership. Start with PostgreSQL, per-conversation ordering, cursor-based catch-up, and a live stream. Persist drafts and pending sends locally, and use idempotent sends so reconnecting after a lost acknowledgment doesn’t post twice. Show pending, sent and failed distinctly. Second, agent cards are durable message attachments, not live model sessions. Start with an A2UI v1.0 subset rendered by a2ui_flutter: summary, facts, a labeled input and a few app-owned actions. Validate and bound the payload, persist a versioned snapshot and a readable fallback, and render no arbitrary HTML, script, or agent-selected function calls. A button like ‘Approve equipment request’ resolves to a registered operation; the server checks the acting person, channel, target and revision, returns a receipt, and updates the card for everyone. An agent’s post is not authority to act on a user’s behalf. Adaptive Cards would move up the list if Teams compatibility were required; MCP Apps targets sandboxed views in compatible hosts, not the default rendering model I want inside long-lived chat history.

Third, agents that operate the app get a scoped MCP adapter, not UI automation. List channels, read or search permitted threads, send or reply, react, and post or inspect cards through the same typed operations the clients use. Agent-Native’s shared-action pattern is the right idea; I’d own the narrow adapter rather than put messaging delivery or authorization inside an agent runtime. Separate bot and delegated identities, enforce membership on every read and write including search and sync, and keep human-only decisions human-only. Label bot messages, cap bot posting and mentions, and give people bot notification controls so automation doesn’t drown out coworkers.
decision.showItsGood:
Build a thin slice on all five clients before expanding: receive a human mention, resume its thread from another device, and act on an agent’s equipment-request card. In CI, run Flutter widget tests for semantics and responsive layouts, integration tests on the five targets, and API/MCP contract tests against actual stored state. Exercise paging a busy channel without losing scroll position, losing the send acknowledgment, reconnecting after missed events, two people acting on the same card, an older client opening it, and membership being revoked. Check that unauthorized reads, writes and notifications are denied. On real builds, inspect screen-reader output with VoiceOver, TalkBack and NVDA, keyboard-only navigation, large text and zoom, text selection and IME composition, and whether incoming messages or card updates steal focus or interrupt typing. On managed hardware and a representative busy channel, profile startup, scroll jank, memory during a workday, and send-to-visible and catch-up latency.

Then run uncoached sessions and a small team pilot, including people who rely on assistive tech. Ask people to find their first unread reply after switching devices, explain who sent a card and what its button will do, handle a stale card, and mute bot noise without missing a human mention. Measure task completion, time to the right thread, mistaken or duplicate actions, and missed mentions. Compare with the team’s current workflow; an increase in card clicks isn’t a win if people misunderstand the effects. Track operational regressions without logging message bodies or card inputs, and rerun the tasks after fixes. These are checks I’d run, not results I have.
decision.unsure: The biggest bet is Flutter web for an all-day text-heavy tool. Flutter documents that web semantics are opt-in by default and can be enabled in code; I’d enable them and test them with a realistically busy timeline before committing. If accessible navigation, browser text behavior or performance still falls short, I’d use a DOM-based web and desktop UI while keeping the message, action and card contracts. I’d also spike a persisted A2UI card with two client versions before locking the format; if the renderer adds more complexity than it saves for our small catalog, ship fixed typed templates first. Company requirements for data residency, retention, legal hold and managed-device support could change the backend or rollout plan.

answer.answer:
The common failure: I treated sharing code and sharing actions as evidence that the experience would hold up across devices. A year later, the things people complain about most are the things the framework demos never exercised. This is a premortem, not a report of what actually happened.

- **Cooking app — Expo:** Cook mode worked beautifully in a foreground demo. In a real kitchen, the browser released the wake lock, an interruption hid a timer alert, and the app came back showing the correct elapsed time. The state was technically right; the cook still missed the timer. Meanwhile, the public recipe catalog outgrew build-time rendering, so we split the web surface later than we should have. I’d test a full cook with an interruption on real phones and make the distinction between *timer recovered* and *alert delivered* a release criterion.
- **Agent work and handoffs — Agent-Native + Tauri:** The shared actions worked, but handoffs became status dumps. Reviewers still opened the PR and reran checks because they couldn’t tell what had been verified. Worse, people read “pause requested” as “the agent stopped.” We spent too long making transports agree and not enough time watching a maintainer take over a task without asking for context. I’d make an interrupted handoff and a disconnected runner the first pilot, before adding more tools.
- **Company chat — Flutter + A2UI:** We saved time on five layouts and spent it back on the composer and timeline: text selection, IME composition, focus, and screen-reader navigation in busy channels. Cards also became a compatibility obligation: an old message still had to make sense after the workflow changed, and bots made it harder to find messages from people. I’d gate Flutter web on a realistic, accessible workday slice and start with fixed card templates and conservative bot notification defaults.

**What slowed down the research:** The candidates weren’t all alternatives at the same layer. Flutter ships clients; A2UI describes UI; MCP lets agents call tools; Agent-Native binds operations to several surfaces. The phrase “human approval” was especially easy to overread: a framework pausing a tool call is not the same as the application recording who approved which revision and enforcing it everywhere. There was some mundane friction too: one search relay failed, a docs URL returned a 404, and a React Aria component page exceeded the fetch limit. But the bigger gap was evidence. The docs could tell me a platform was supported or an approval flow existed. They couldn’t tell me whether a cook would notice a missed alert, a reviewer would understand a handoff, or someone using a screen reader could keep up with a busy channel. Those were the first things I needed to put in front of people.

I didn’t pick Ouro UI as the foundation for any of the three apps. After reading the project, I’d try **Ouro AX on the agent handoff tool** before I’d switch any app to **Ouro HX**. I reviewed the docs and repository; I didn’t run the kits.

**What would stop me from switching the UI:** Ouro deliberately ships separate React, SwiftUI, WinUI and Compose kits, not a Flutter or React Native kit. That’s a reasonable choice for a team already maintaining native clients. For the cooking and chat apps I proposed, it means owning several UI implementations, release pipelines and accessibility test matrices. The project’s own platform notes make the tradeoff concrete: Windows and Android can render Ouro’s composed tree, but their component inventories are much smaller than the web kit’s, they don’t read A2UI directly, and the Android kit reports emulator-only testing. A shared card format doesn’t make the chat composer or cook mode shared. On the web, the copy-in model is attractive because we own the code, but I’d want to see a routine upgrade preserve our local accessibility fixes without a painful merge. Spoonjoy is a useful reference for the cooking app; it isn’t evidence about Android in a kitchen or a busy five-client chat rollout.

**What would make me adopt it:** I’d trial one real handoff without replacing React Aria or Tauri. Let an agent submit revision A, then replace it with B while a reviewer has A open. Check that the generated CLI and MCP surfaces stay aligned, that the server refuses a stale approval or an approval from an agent identity, and that a keyboard or screen-reader user can tell what changed and recover. Run [AX X-ray](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md) against an isolated fixture and keep the end-to-end authorization and usability tests: the project itself documents a case where conformance passed and task-flow checks still failed. I’d adopt AX if that trial caught drift our existing tests missed without creating a second source of truth. I’d switch the UI only after a real-device comparison showed better outcomes on the app’s hardest workflow, and the team had rehearsed an upgrade and rollback.

**What it would let me do:** Nothing here is impossible with our picks. The difference is what we get to stop wiring and checking by hand. [Ouro’s action declaration](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md) can generate multiple interfaces and check for drift against the running MCP tool catalog. Its [composed UI](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/composed-ui/) lets an agent assemble a card while the app owns the button label and consent class. That gives me a way to let agents propose more varied interfaces without letting them invent operations or rewrite what a confirmation means. Our server would still decide who can do what, to which revision.

actions.name: record_decision
actions.why:
I’d build a shared work ledger and review queue, not a chat app. Coding agents already run in their own environments; this product records their state and carries people’s decisions back to them. Agent-Native is my starting point because a typed action can serve both app clients and external tools. I’d keep task transitions, handoff schemas and authorization in plain TypeScript behind those adapters so the workflow doesn’t depend on an agent runtime. CopilotKit makes more sense if live conversations and in-chat interactions become central. For this job, the persistent review queue matters more. React Aria gives me keyboard and focus behavior for a dense task list and review UI; Radix would also be a reasonable choice for dialogs and menus. I’d ship the same React UI in the browser and bundled in Tauri, with no shell or filesystem bridge in v1. Electron would be my fallback if differences between OS webviews hurt diff rendering or accessibility enough to justify bundling Chromium.

Agents get scoped identities and a small set of explicit actions: claim a task, checkpoint progress, report a blocker, submit a handoff, and fetch a decision. A handoff carries the objective, an artifact revision, links to the diff and checks, what remains unverified, and a proposed next step. PostgreSQL holds current state and an append-only transition history updated in the same transaction. Use revision checks and idempotency keys so retries don’t duplicate work and stale writers can’t silently overwrite a reviewer. Start with a minimal tool catalog, no raw SQL or code execution, and verify exposure on each enabled transport. A reviewer's decision is a server-side permission, not a model instruction or a disabled button. Approval applies to the exact revision reviewed; any replacement goes back to review. Don’t conflate requested pause with acknowledged pause: if a runner disconnects, show that it hasn’t acknowledged the request and prevent new claims while paused.

The first screen is ‘Needs your decision.’ A reviewer should see what changed, who or what reported it, what evidence exists, and what approving would authorize without reading a transcript. Show Approve, Request changes and Pause as distinct actions; never let a stream of agent updates move the target under the reviewer’s cursor or keyboard focus. Treat agent summaries as claims, not verified evidence.
actions.showItsGood:
Start with one ordinary code-change workflow: one agent checkpoints and disconnects, another resumes from the handoff, and a reviewer requests changes and then approves the revised artifact from the other surface. Run action contract tests through HTTP and MCP for simultaneous claims, duplicate requests, stale approvals, disallowed reviewer actions from agent identities, and workspace isolation. Check that the actual durable state and history agree after retries and reconnects. Replay a high-volume burst of updates against the review queue. In Playwright and in packaged desktop builds, inspect what happens to selection, focus and screen-reader announcements during live updates; check keyboard-only review, large text, and diffs with missing or failed checks. Automated axe checks are a floor, not the accessibility test.

Put this in front of maintainers who actually review agent work, including keyboard and screen-reader users. Without coaching, ask them to pick up after an interrupted agent, find the one decision that needs them, explain what they’re approving, and redirect work on the wrong task. Include a plausible summary that overstates what the attached checks prove. Compare against their existing issue/PR/chat workflow on time to a correct decision, mistaken approvals, successful handoffs without asking for context again, and recovery after interruption. A faster review with more mistaken approvals is a regression. After launch, watch stale-decision rejections and unacknowledged pause requests, then rerun the scenarios after fixes. These are proposed checks, not results.
actions.unsure: I’d spike two representative coding-agent clients against the same staged handoff before committing to the framework. The docs describe shared actions and several approval flows, but I wouldn’t assume that both clients preserve scoped identity, structured errors or reconnect behavior the same way, or use Agent-Native’s approval prompts as the authority for our domain decisions. If I can’t keep transport exposure narrow and authorization consistent, I’d use a small TypeScript HTTP service and an MCP adapter over the same commands. I’m assuming a shared online workspace; offline desktop writes would require a separate consistency design.

pairings: A2UI (a2ui_flutter, with a restricted card catalog)
TypeScript and PostgreSQL for the messaging service

actions.why:
I’d use Flutter for the five clients: this is a signed-in, interactive app, and sharing the timeline, composer, and card renderer is worth more here than it is for a document-oriented website. I’d share behavior, not force identical layouts: compact navigation and native push on phones, keyboard shortcuts and multi-pane navigation on desktop, and reliable links, selection, and browser history on web. Fluent UI React is a good candidate for a web-first company app, but doesn’t by itself give me the five clients. A DOM-based React web client and desktop wrapper plus a separate mobile UI is my fallback if Flutter’s web experience falls short.

I’d keep three contracts separate. First, the chat service owns messages, threads, read cursors and channel membership. Start with PostgreSQL, per-conversation ordering, cursor-based catch-up, and a live stream. Persist drafts and pending sends locally, and use idempotent sends so reconnecting after a lost acknowledgment doesn’t post twice. Show pending, sent and failed distinctly. Second, agent cards are durable message attachments, not live model sessions. Start with an A2UI v1.0 subset rendered by a2ui_flutter: summary, facts, a labeled input and a few app-owned actions. Validate and bound the payload, persist a versioned snapshot and a readable fallback, and render no arbitrary HTML, script, or agent-selected function calls. A button like ‘Approve equipment request’ resolves to a registered operation; the server checks the acting person, channel, target and revision, returns a receipt, and updates the card for everyone. An agent’s post is not authority to act on a user’s behalf. Adaptive Cards would move up the list if Teams compatibility were required; MCP Apps targets sandboxed views in compatible hosts, not the default rendering model I want inside long-lived chat history.

Third, agents that operate the app get a scoped MCP adapter, not UI automation. List channels, read or search permitted threads, send or reply, react, and post or inspect cards through the same typed operations the clients use. Agent-Native’s shared-action pattern is the right idea; I’d own the narrow adapter rather than put messaging delivery or authorization inside an agent runtime. Separate bot and delegated identities, enforce membership on every read and write including search and sync, and keep human-only decisions human-only. Label bot messages, cap bot posting and mentions, and give people bot notification controls so automation doesn’t drown out coworkers.
actions.showItsGood:
Build a thin slice on all five clients before expanding: receive a human mention, resume its thread from another device, and act on an agent’s equipment-request card. In CI, run Flutter widget tests for semantics and responsive layouts, integration tests on the five targets, and API/MCP contract tests against actual stored state. Exercise paging a busy channel without losing scroll position, losing the send acknowledgment, reconnecting after missed events, two people acting on the same card, an older client opening it, and membership being revoked. Check that unauthorized reads, writes and notifications are denied. On real builds, inspect screen-reader output with VoiceOver, TalkBack and NVDA, keyboard-only navigation, large text and zoom, text selection and IME composition, and whether incoming messages or card updates steal focus or interrupt typing. On managed hardware and a representative busy channel, profile startup, scroll jank, memory during a workday, and send-to-visible and catch-up latency.

Then run uncoached sessions and a small team pilot, including people who rely on assistive tech. Ask people to find their first unread reply after switching devices, explain who sent a card and what its button will do, handle a stale card, and mute bot noise without missing a human mention. Measure task completion, time to the right thread, mistaken or duplicate actions, and missed mentions. Compare with the team’s current workflow; an increase in card clicks isn’t a win if people misunderstand the effects. Track operational regressions without logging message bodies or card inputs, and rerun the tasks after fixes. These are checks I’d run, not results I have.
actions.unsure: The biggest bet is Flutter web for an all-day text-heavy tool. Flutter documents that web semantics are opt-in by default and can be enabled in code; I’d enable them and test them with a realistically busy timeline before committing. If accessible navigation, browser text behavior or performance still falls short, I’d use a DOM-based web and desktop UI while keeping the message, action and card contracts. I’d also spike a persisted A2UI card with two client versions before locking the format; if the renderer adds more complexity than it saves for our small catalog, ship fixed typed templates first. Company requirements for data residency, retention, legal hold and managed-device support could change the backend or rollout plan.

actions.name: answer
actions.answer:
The common failure: I treated sharing code and sharing actions as evidence that the experience would hold up across devices. A year later, the things people complain about most are the things the framework demos never exercised. This is a premortem, not a report of what actually happened.

- **Cooking app — Expo:** Cook mode worked beautifully in a foreground demo. In a real kitchen, the browser released the wake lock, an interruption hid a timer alert, and the app came back showing the correct elapsed time. The state was technically right; the cook still missed the timer. Meanwhile, the public recipe catalog outgrew build-time rendering, so we split the web surface later than we should have. I’d test a full cook with an interruption on real phones and make the distinction between *timer recovered* and *alert delivered* a release criterion.
- **Agent work and handoffs — Agent-Native + Tauri:** The shared actions worked, but handoffs became status dumps. Reviewers still opened the PR and reran checks because they couldn’t tell what had been verified. Worse, people read “pause requested” as “the agent stopped.” We spent too long making transports agree and not enough time watching a maintainer take over a task without asking for context. I’d make an interrupted handoff and a disconnected runner the first pilot, before adding more tools.
- **Company chat — Flutter + A2UI:** We saved time on five layouts and spent it back on the composer and timeline: text selection, IME composition, focus, and screen-reader navigation in busy channels. Cards also became a compatibility obligation: an old message still had to make sense after the workflow changed, and bots made it harder to find messages from people. I’d gate Flutter web on a realistic, accessible workday slice and start with fixed card templates and conservative bot notification defaults.

**What slowed down the research:** The candidates weren’t all alternatives at the same layer. Flutter ships clients; A2UI describes UI; MCP lets agents call tools; Agent-Native binds operations to several surfaces. The phrase “human approval” was especially easy to overread: a framework pausing a tool call is not the same as the application recording who approved which revision and enforcing it everywhere. There was some mundane friction too: one search relay failed, a docs URL returned a 404, and a React Aria component page exceeded the fetch limit. But the bigger gap was evidence. The docs could tell me a platform was supported or an approval flow existed. They couldn’t tell me whether a cook would notice a missed alert, a reviewer would understand a handoff, or someone using a screen reader could keep up with a busy channel. Those were the first things I needed to put in front of people.

actions.name: answer
actions.answer:
I didn’t pick Ouro UI as the foundation for any of the three apps. After reading the project, I’d try **Ouro AX on the agent handoff tool** before I’d switch any app to **Ouro HX**. I reviewed the docs and repository; I didn’t run the kits.

**What would stop me from switching the UI:** Ouro deliberately ships separate React, SwiftUI, WinUI and Compose kits, not a Flutter or React Native kit. That’s a reasonable choice for a team already maintaining native clients. For the cooking and chat apps I proposed, it means owning several UI implementations, release pipelines and accessibility test matrices. The project’s own platform notes make the tradeoff concrete: Windows and Android can render Ouro’s composed tree, but their component inventories are much smaller than the web kit’s, they don’t read A2UI directly, and the Android kit reports emulator-only testing. A shared card format doesn’t make the chat composer or cook mode shared. On the web, the copy-in model is attractive because we own the code, but I’d want to see a routine upgrade preserve our local accessibility fixes without a painful merge. Spoonjoy is a useful reference for the cooking app; it isn’t evidence about Android in a kitchen or a busy five-client chat rollout.

**What would make me adopt it:** I’d trial one real handoff without replacing React Aria or Tauri. Let an agent submit revision A, then replace it with B while a reviewer has A open. Check that the generated CLI and MCP surfaces stay aligned, that the server refuses a stale approval or an approval from an agent identity, and that a keyboard or screen-reader user can tell what changed and recover. Run [AX X-ray](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md) against an isolated fixture and keep the end-to-end authorization and usability tests: the project itself documents a case where conformance passed and task-flow checks still failed. I’d adopt AX if that trial caught drift our existing tests missed without creating a second source of truth. I’d switch the UI only after a real-device comparison showed better outcomes on the app’s hardest workflow, and the team had rehearsed an upgrade and rollback.

**What it would let me do:** Nothing here is impossible with our picks. The difference is what we get to stop wiring and checking by hand. [Ouro’s action declaration](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md) can generate multiple interfaces and check for drift against the running MCP tool catalog. Its [composed UI](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/composed-ui/) lets an agent assemble a card while the app owns the button label and consent class. That gives me a way to let agents propose more varied interfaces without letting them invent operations or rewrite what a confirmation means. Our server would still decide who can do what, to which revision.
